new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (22,098 lines). The quoted passage is at lines 3185-3194, immediately under the heading '3.4 Tone and Stress' (line 3174), on the page following the '70 LANGUAGES OF ZAMBIA' running head (line 3159) and before 'SKETCH OF THE BANTU LANGUAGES 71' (line 3204), so the locator 'p. 70 (continues p. 71)' is right. The text matches the report's quote word for word except for scanned artefacts that the reader silently normalised: 'vv' for 'w' (hovvever, vovvel, vvords, vvhich), 'syilable' for 'syllable'. The 'earlier rule' referred to is on pp. 63-64 (lines 2871-2879): 'in all the languages of the Eastern Province (including Nyanja), and in several languages of the Northwestern Province, the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Generalisation over the Zambian Bantu languages surveyed (Inamwanga, Iwa and Tambo among them): no distinctive word stress; syllables roughly evenly prominent, with at most a slight penultimate prominence in some languages that the authors attribute to penultimate vowel lengthening; every syllable carries one of two tones, high or low (pp. 70-71: 'A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone.. There are only two contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low'). For Nyamwanga specifically the only prosodic statements found are tonal: Siame 2022 p. 124 ('LuMaNa are tonal languages which have two basic tones, namely, high and low') and, second-hand via Siame 2022 p. 115, Bickmore 2000's phrase-penultimate vowel lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate prominence is given only as a tendency 'in some languages (e.g. Cewa)', not asserted for Nyamwanga; penultimate lengthening is said to be a standard rule in Eastern and some North-Western Province languages (pp. 63-64), not stated for Nyamwanga; Siame 2022 disputes Bickmore's non-contrastive-length claim for Namwanga.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('syllables in the same word'); the statement covers 'Zambian languages' as a class, drawn from the authors' comparative survey whose sample includes Inamwanga, Iwa and Tambo, but the passage does not name Nyamwanga. Bickmore's penultimate lengthening (as reported by Siame 2022) is at the level of the phonological phrase.
new_statements.identity_note: Kashoki & Mann 1978 describe 'Zambian languages' as a class; their sample includes Inamwanga, Iwa and Tambo (all = nyam1275 per Glottolog). Siame 2022 and the Daengku papers describe Zambian Namwanga of Nakonde and Isoka districts (Chieftainess Waitwika / Chief Kafwimbi areas), i.e. the Zambian variety, not the Tanzanian Inamwanga that Busse 1940/41 described. Bickmore 2000 is Zambian Namwanga (Northern Province). Dialects Iwa and Tambo are subsumed under nyam1275; no dialect-specific statement was found.

sources.note: For Zambian languages generally (Inamwanga, Iwa and Tambo are among the languages surveyed): syllables are more or less evenly stressed; in some languages (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems slightly more forceful, possibly just an effect of penultimate lengthening; stress never distinguishes words; every syllable carries one of two tones (H/L). Nyamwanga is not named in the passage itself.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement on stress placement. p. 124: 'LuMaNa are tonal languages which have two basic tones, namely, high and low' (minimal pairs iká/íká etc.). p. 115 reports second-hand that 'Bickmore (2000) claims that vowel length is not contrastive in Namwanga instead there is a predictable process by which a penultimate vowel of a phonological phrase becomes lengthened', and argues against it that length is phonemic in Namwanga. The only use of 'stresses' (p. 291) concerns reciprocal verb morphology, not prosody.
